cues.text: Welcome to Atomic Structure.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Atomic number counts protons and fixes the element.
Mass number counts protons plus neutrons in a particular isotope.
Subtract atomic number from mass number to find neutrons.
For aluminium twenty seven, atomic number thirteen, there are thirteen protons
and fourteen neutrons.
An aluminium three plus ion has lost three electrons, leaving ten.
Ordinary ionization does not change the nucleus.
Isotopes share the same proton number but have different neutron numbers.
Isobars share mass number, while isotones share neutron number.
Check the actual counts rather than relying on similar names.
The periodic table's relative atomic mass is usually an isotope weighted
average, not the mass number of one atom.
Imagine an element with isotopes of relative masses ten and eleven, present in
twenty and eighty percent proportions.
The weighted mean is zero point two times ten plus zero point eight times
eleven, or ten point eight.
This does not imply that each atom contains a fractional neutron.
Rutherford scattering supported a tiny, positively charged nucleus and a
largely empty atomic volume, but a classical planetary picture did not explain
stable atomic energies.
In vacuum, frequency times wavelength equals the speed of light.
Photon energy equals Planck's constant times frequency, or h c divided by
wavelength.
Shorter wavelength means more energy per photon, not faster travel through
vacuum.
With h c equal to twelve hundred forty electron volt nanometres, a four
hundred
nanometre photon carries three point one zero electron volts.
If a surface work function is two point zero zero electron volts, the maximum
photoelectron kinetic energy is one point one zero electron volts.
The stopping potential magnitude is one point one zero volts.
Below the threshold frequency, increasing ordinary light intensity cannot
overcome the per photon energy deficit in the elementary single photon model.
Above threshold, intensity can increase the photon arrival rate and
photocurrent under fixed collection conditions; frequency controls maximum
electron energy.
A second example uses six hundred twenty nanometre light and work function one
point five zero electron volts.
Photon energy is two point zero zero electron volts, leaving zero point five
zero electron volts of maximum kinetic energy.
Always match units: using Planck's constant in joule seconds requires
wavelength in metres and energies in joules.
Do not confuse energy of one photon with the total energy delivered by a beam.
Bohr postulated stationary states and angular momentum equal to an integer
times h bar.
For a one electron ion, Coulomb attraction supplies the centripetal force in
this historical model.
Combining the force equation with angular momentum quantization gives radius
proportional to n squared divided by nuclear charge Z.
Kinetic energy is half the magnitude of potential energy, so the total bound
state energy is negative.
The introductory expressions are radius equals a zero times n squared divided
by Z, and energy equals minus thirteen point six times Z squared divided by
n squared, in electron volts.
These describe hydrogen and one electron ions, not neutral helium or general
many electron atoms.
For helium plus with Z equal to two and n equal to two, radius is zero point
zero five two nine times four divided by two nanometres, or zero point one
zero
five eight nanometres.
Energy is minus thirteen point six electron volts.
Raising n makes a bound energy less negative and increases the model radius.
The separated electron and nucleus define the zero energy continuum.
The formulas neglect reduced mass and relativistic corrections.
Modern quantum mechanics replaces fixed circular electron tracks with states
described by wavefunctions.
Use Bohr formulas for their stated one electron calculations without treating
the orbits as modern probability pictures.
An emitted photon carries the positive difference between the initial atomic
energy and the lower final energy.
Absorption requires a photon matching an allowed upward energy difference.
For hydrogen falling from level four to level two, the photon energy is
thirteen point six times one quarter minus one sixteenth, or two point five
five electron volts.
Dividing twelve hundred forty by two point five five gives wavelength about
four hundred eighty six nanometres.
This belongs to the Balmer series because the lower level is two.
Lyman transitions have lower level one, and Paschen transitions have lower
level three.
The Rydberg expression places the lower level term first so the inverse
wavelength is positive.
Ionization means reaching the zero energy continuum, not merely moving up one
bound level.
Hydrogen initially in level two has energy minus three point four zero
electron
volts, so it needs three point four zero electron volts to ionize.
The ground state needs thirteen point six.
For the same pair of principal levels in a hydrogen like ion, transition
energy
scales as Z squared and wavelength scales inversely as Z squared.
Keep the charge state, initial level and final level visible throughout the
calculation.
De Broglie's relation assigns wavelength h divided by momentum to a particle.
A nonrelativistic electron accelerated from rest through a voltage gains
kinetic energy equal to electron charge times voltage.
Its momentum is the square root of two times mass times that energy.
Combining these relations gives the familiar electron shortcut: wavelength in
angstroms is approximately twelve point two seven divided by the square root
of
voltage in volts.
At one hundred volts it is one point two two seven angstroms.
At four hundred volts it is zero point six one three five angstroms.
Quadrupling voltage doubles momentum and halves wavelength.
This low speed approximation is not suitable at arbitrarily high voltages.
Matter waves are not electromagnetic waves travelling at the speed of light.
The uncertainty relation says the position standard deviation times the
matching momentum standard deviation is at least h bar over two.
These are spreads in a quantum state, not simply the least count of measuring
instruments.
Halving position spread doubles the minimum allowed momentum spread.
With position spread ten to the minus ten metres, the lower momentum spread is
about five point two seven five times ten to the minus twenty five kilogram
metres per second.
An orbital is a quantum state described by a wavefunction.
Its squared magnitude gives probability density; it is not a tiny planetary
track.
The principal quantum number n is a positive integer.
For a chosen n, the angular momentum quantum number l ranges from zero to n
minus one.
Labels s, p, d and f correspond to zero, one, two and three.
A two d subshell is impossible because n equal to two allows only s and p.
For a specified l, the magnetic quantum number takes integer values from minus
l to plus l, giving two l plus one orbitals.
A three d subshell therefore has five orbitals, with magnetic values minus
two,
minus one, zero, plus one and plus two.
Each orbital holds at most two electrons with opposite spin quantum numbers.
Pauli's exclusion principle forbids two electrons in an atom from sharing all
four quantum numbers.
The s, p, d and f subshell capacities are two, six, ten and fourteen.
Summing the orbital counts within shell n gives n squared orbitals and a
maximum of two n squared electrons.
Shell three has nine orbitals and capacity eighteen.
Capacity does not imply that all shells fill completely in principal number
order.
An s orbital has spherical angular symmetry.
A real p orbital is commonly pictured with two lobes on opposite sides of a
nodal plane through the nucleus.
The two colours in an orbital drawing usually indicate opposite wavefunction
signs, not positive and negative electric charges.
Squaring the wavefunction removes that sign from probability density.
Most familiar real d orbitals have four lobes; the d z squared picture has two
lobes and a ring.
These sketches show chosen probability boundaries, not hard walls.
In the hydrogen like orbital model, angular nodes number l and radial nodes
number n minus l minus one.
Their total is n minus one.
For a three p orbital, n is three and l is one: there is one radial node and
one angular node.
For three d, there are zero radial nodes and two angular nodes.
A two s orbital has one radial node and no angular node.
A radial probability distribution includes the volume factor associated with
spherical shells, so it is not the same graph as probability density at a
point.
Node counting and these distinctions are a foundation; detailed radial
wavefunction and distribution plots need separate practice.
Ground state configurations use lower available energy states first, with
Pauli's two electron limit and Hund's rule for equal energy orbitals.
Hund filling puts one electron in each degenerate orbital with parallel spins
before pairing.
Nitrogen has three singly occupied two p orbitals.
Oxygen has one pair and two unpaired two p electrons.
The n plus l ordering rule is a useful introductory guide: smaller n plus l
comes first, and for a tie smaller n comes first.
It is not an exact universal energy law.
Neutral chromium is conventionally written argon core, three d five, four s
one; copper is argon core, three d ten, four s one.
These differ from a naive filling sequence because nearby subshell energies
and
electron interactions matter.
Do not turn half filled or filled stability into a rule overriding measured
configurations in every case.
Neutral iron is argon core, three d six, four s two.
Forming its common cations removes four s electrons before three d electrons.
Iron two plus is three d six beyond the argon core, and iron three plus is
three d five.
Always count the final electrons: iron three plus has twenty three.
Magnetic behaviour of a free ion and that of its coordination complexes can
differ.
Exciting an atom and ionizing it are different energy changes.
Begin with hydrogen in its ground state at minus thirteen point six electron
volts.
Absorbing ten point two electron volts raises its energy to minus three point
four, corresponding to principal level two.
The electron remains bound because its energy is still negative relative to
the
stated continuum.
Removing it from that excited level requires another three point four electron
volts.
These two steps add to the ground state ionization energy, thirteen point six.
A photon below the remaining ionization threshold cannot ionize this isolated
atom in the elementary single photon model, although it may match an allowed
bound transition.
For a one electron helium ion, nuclear charge is two, so all these level
energies scale by four within the hydrogen like approximation.
Its level two energy is therefore minus thirteen point six electron volts and
ionization from that level requires positive thirteen point six.
Specify the initial state before quoting an ionization energy.
Do not use the ground state threshold automatically for an excited atom or
apply one electron formulas to neutral helium.
A spectral line corresponds to an energy difference, not simply to the number
written on an excited level.
Consider many hydrogen atoms prepared in principal level four.
Across an ensemble that can populate all lower levels through allowed
cascades,
the elementary level model permits six distinct principal level differences:
four to three, four to two, four to one, three to two, three to one and two to
one.
The pair count is four times three divided by two.
This is a maximum set across the ensemble, not a promise that one atom emits
six photons.
A single downward sequence from four through three and two to one contains
three emissions.
A direct four to one transition emits just one.
For the four to two Balmer line, energy is thirteen point six times one
quarter
minus one sixteenth, giving two point five five electron volts.
With the supplied conversion twelve hundred forty electron volt nanometres,
its
wavelength is about four hundred eighty six point three nanometres.
Selection rules and experimental populations affect which lines appear.
Keep the simplified principal level counting assumption separate from a claim
about every detailed atomic transition.
A restricted quantum number question requires counting the permitted states
rather than substituting the full shell capacity automatically.
In principal shell four, angular quantum number can be zero, one, two or
three.
If the question allows only angular values two and three, the available
subshells are four d and four f.
They contain five and seven spatial orbitals, so together they can hold twenty
four electrons.
The familiar full shell capacity thirty two includes the excluded s and p
states and would be wrong here.
In shell three, suppose the magnetic quantum number must be zero.
Each of the three allowed angular values has one such orbital, giving three
orbitals and at most six electrons.
If spin is also fixed to plus one half, only one of the two spin states in
each
orbital remains, so the count becomes three electrons.
Count allowed angular values, then magnetic values, then spin choices.
Pauli exclusion limits occupation of each complete state, and the capacity
calculation does not imply that every permitted state is occupied in a
particular ground state atom.
Orbital node questions distinguish radial and angular structure.
A hydrogen like orbital has angular node count equal to angular quantum
number,
radial node count equal to principal number minus angular number minus one,
and
total node count principal number minus one.
For a three p orbital, angular number is one.
There is one radial node and one angular node, giving two in total.
For a four d orbital, angular number is two, leaving one radial node and two
angular nodes, or three total.
A node is a region where the wavefunction is zero; the probability density is
also zero there.
A sign change in an orbital drawing indicates wavefunction phase, not positive
versus negative electric charge.
Do not count a radial probability maximum as a node.
Also distinguish the radial wavefunction from the radial probability
distribution, which includes the spherical volume factor.
The zero of that volume factor at the origin is not an extra spherical radial
node in this standard counting rule.
Use these counts within the stated hydrogen like orbital description rather
than treating every approximate many electron orbital as exactly the same
mathematical function.
The uncertainty relation gives a lower bound on the product of position and
momentum spreads.
It does not state that an electron follows a classical orbit with an unknown
but exact radius.
Suppose position spread is one times ten to the minus ten metre.
Using reduced Planck constant one point zero five five times ten to the minus
thirty four joule second, the minimum momentum spread is about five point two
seven five times ten to the minus twenty five kilogram metre per second.
Dividing by the supplied electron mass nine point one one times ten to the
minus thirty one kilogram gives a minimum velocity spread about five point
seven nine times ten to the five metres per second in the nonrelativistic
relation.
This is a spread, not the electron's measured speed or mean velocity.
Halving position spread doubles the minimum momentum spread.
Equality is attained only for suitable minimum uncertainty states; it is not
automatic for an arbitrary wavefunction.
State which uncertainty convention is used, preserve the factor of two, and
compare dimensions before interpreting the result.
This limitation comes from the quantum description rather than merely from
careless measurement equipment.
In the elementary nonrelativistic one electron Coulomb model, all orbitals
with
the same principal quantum number have the same energy.
For the shell with n equal to three, the allowed subshells are three s, three
p
and three d.
They contain one, three and five spatial orbitals respectively, giving nine
orbitals in total.
Including the two possible spin states per orbital gives eighteen one electron
spin states for that shell.
This state count is not eighteen electrons actually present in a hydrogen
atom;
hydrogen has one electron whose state can be selected from the allowed
possibilities.
The same simple degeneracy applies to a hydrogen like one electron ion when
the
nuclear charge changes the energy scale.
It does not transfer unchanged to a general many electron atom, where electron
repulsion, shielding and penetration separate subshell energies.
External fields and finer relativistic or spin dependent corrections can also
split levels that the elementary model treats as equal.
State whether the question asks for orbitals, spin states or actual occupied
electrons before multiplying by two.
The n squared spatial orbital count and twice n squared shell capacity are
related statements, not interchangeable answers to every counting question.
For a hydrogen like one s state, probability density per unit volume is
largest
at the nucleus and decreases exponentially with distance.
A radial distribution asks a different question: how much probability lies in
a
thin spherical shell at a given radius.
The shell volume includes a factor proportional to radius squared.
Consequently the radial distribution is zero at zero radius, rises to a
maximum, and then falls, even though the density per unit volume is largest at
the origin.
Define the dimensionless radius x as nuclear charge times radius divided by
the
Bohr radius.
The normalized radial distribution with respect to x is four x squared times
the exponential of minus two x.
Its maximum occurs at x equal to one, so the most probable radius in this one
s
model is the Bohr radius divided by nuclear charge.
For hydrogen this is about zero point five two nine angstrom, while a one
electron helium ion gives half that radius.
This maximum is neither a fixed classical orbit nor the radius containing all
probability.
Probability over an interval requires integrating the distribution, and the
mean radius is a different statistical quantity.
Electron configuration questions should distinguish an allowed excited state
from a violation of orbital capacity.
A neutral neon atom has ten electrons.
Its familiar ground configuration fills one s, two s and two p as two, two and
six electrons.
A configuration with two electrons in one s, two in two s, five in two p and
one in three s still totals ten.
It respects the maximum of two electrons in an individual spatial orbital and
can represent an excited configuration, although it is not the ground state.
By contrast, writing three electrons in one s violates the Pauli capacity of
that single spatial orbital even if another occupancy is adjusted to preserve
the total electron count.
The Aufbau filling order is a ground state organizing principle, so a promoted
electron is not automatically evidence of a physically impossible state.
A subshell occupancy alone may not specify one unique spin state or all
details
of the actual energy eigenstate.
Check the task's level of description: count electrons, check available
orbitals and spin restrictions, then decide whether ground state ordering is
required.
An invalid quantum number set cannot be repaired simply by calling it excited.
Hydrogen like spectra can identify a nuclear charge only after the one
electron
model and transition are supplied.
Suppose a photon of seventeen point zero electron volts is emitted by a one
electron ion falling from principal level three to level two.
In the elementary model, the energy difference is thirteen point six times
nuclear charge squared times one quarter minus one ninth, in electron volts.
The bracket is five thirty sixths.
Dividing seventeen by thirteen point six times that bracket gives nuclear
charge squared equal to nine, so the positive nuclear charge number is three.
The species is therefore lithium with two electrons removed, leaving one
electron.
It is not neutral lithium, which has three electrons and does not obey this
simple one electron energy formula.
Using the supplied photon relation twelve hundred forty electron volt
nanometres gives wavelength about seventy two point nine four nanometres.
The photon energy is positive while the atom's energy change during emission
is
negative by the same magnitude.
Finite nuclear mass and finer corrections are neglected here.
The calculation identifies a model consistent ion from the specified line; it
does not infer a complete spectrum from one unlabelled measured wavelength.
